pll1d19c9-d1e3477.summary: With Augustine, the three persons are not one essence as three men alike in sex, body, and mind are one nature: among men three are more than one and two more than one, as with statues, but in God Father and Son together are not a greater essence than either; the three are equal to each.
claims: Three men of one nature are more than one man.
In God, three persons together are equal to each one.

pll1d19c9-d1e3496.summary: Concludes that the three persons are called the divine essence neither by material cause (statues and gold), nor by likeness of composition (men of one nature), nor as genus of species or species of individuals, that is, as container of contents or greater of lesser.
claims: The persons are not one essence by matter, likeness of complexion, or predicable relation.

pll1d19c9-d1e3499.summary: Notes that some Catholic writers seem to teach the opposite, that the divine essence is something common and universal like a species and the persons three particulars differing in number.

pll1d19c9-d1e3503.summary: Cites John Damascene, in the version Pope Eugenius had translated: universals are predicated of their particulars; substance is common, hypostasis (person) particular, not as having part of the nature but as numerically one, an individual; hypostases differ in number, not nature.
claims: Damascene says substance is common and hypostasis particular.
Damascene says hypostases differ in number, not nature.

pll1d19c9-d1e3524.summary: Further Damascene: substance signifies a common, embracing species of hypostases alike in species, such as God or man; hypostasis signifies the individual, such as Father, Son, Spirit, or Peter and Paul. This seems wholly contrary to Augustine. Lombard says that what Augustine taught must be held without hesitation.
claims: Damascene calls God a species and the persons individuals.
This seems to contradict Augustine.
Augustine's teaching is to be held without hesitation.

pll1d19c9-d1e3548.summary: Says Damascene's words, though on the surface they sound alien to the faith, can be understood soundly and demand a pious reader; he would rather listen in silence than give the malicious occasion to detract by speaking.
claims: Damascene's words can be understood soundly.
They require a pious reader.

pll1d19c9-d1e3551.summary: Offers an interpretation: Damascene did not use 'common' and 'particular' of God as in philosophy, but by likeness. As the universal is predicated of many and the individual of one, so the divine essence is called universal because predicated of all persons together and each separately, and each person particular because predicated of none of the others. He called the essence a common species because, as 'man' is predicated of Peter and Paul who do not differ in species, so 'God' is predicated of persons who do not differ in divinity. Damascene, weighing the likeness, transferred the terms; Augustine, seeing greater unlikeness, removed them from the Trinity.
claims: Damascene used the terms by analogy of predication.
The essence is predicated of all persons and of each; each person is predicated of none of the others.
Damascene emphasized likeness; Augustine emphasized unlikeness.

pl-l1d19c9.summary: Adds that the persons are not one essence as three men alike in sex, body, and mind are of one nature, since three men are more than one, but in God two persons are not more essence than one. So the persons are called the divine essence neither by material cause, nor by likeness of composition, nor as genus of species or species of individuals. Lombard then faces John Damascene, whose De fide orthodoxa calls substance common and universal and hypostasis particular, persons differing in number, with God a species like man. Augustine's teaching must be held without hesitation. Damascene's words sound foreign to the faith but can be understood soundly: he speaks by likeness to the philosophers, calling essence universal because it is predicated of all persons together and of each, and each person particular because it is predicated of none of the others. Damascene transferred these terms because of the likeness; Augustine, seeing more unlikeness, removed them.
claims: The persons are not one essence as three men are of one nature.
Three human beings are more than one; three divine persons are not more than one.
The persons are not called one essence by material cause, by likeness of composition, or as genus or species.
John Damascene calls the divine substance universal and the hypostases particular.
Augustine's teaching is to be held without hesitation.
Damascene used 'universal' and 'particular' by likeness of predication, not in the philosophical sense.
Damascene stressed the likeness to temporal things; Augustine stressed the greater unlikeness.
concepts: harmonization of Greek and Latin authorities
